normalized.governing_thought: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Scale the software business, which reaches profitability within current cash, and sell fast delivery to grocers
executive_summary: Answer: No. As an operator, Parcelbird would lose money on every order at any level of performance observed so far, and the plan would break the board's cash rules within a year. The software business has a funded path to profit and still captures the growth in quick commerce.
A. The economics fail: the market grows but makes no profit, and a Parcelbird order would lose money
The market grew 41% a year to $5.1B (2022–25), but both incumbents lose money on each order; QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities
At the median of Parcelbird's 14 customer sites, an order loses $6.17 after site costs. The best composite still loses $1.76, and the pop-up lost $12.57
The plan's +$2.02 needs every driver to beat the best site ever observed. At the standard 6% promotions it falls to +$0.22
With $38 CAC and 22% of customers left at month 3, acquisition cost is never earned back at benchmark economics
B. Parcelbird cannot afford to find out: every dark-store option breaks the 12-month runway floor
If the $9.5M plan runs on top of today's software burn, runway falls below 12 months in month 2 and cash runs out in month 15
At benchmark economics, nine stores need about $37M in their first full year (operating loss, CAC, capex) against $12M of cash, and no new round is expected
Even a one-store pilot (about $3.8M) keeps runway below 12 months from month 5 to month 18
C. Scaling the software business is the better route into the same market
The pipeline holds $3.55M of ARR, 1.4× what 60% growth needs in 2027. The $0.8M/yr of hires pay back with about 11 contracts
Base case: cash break-even in about month 26, cash never below $5.4M, runway never below 24 months. Holds at 45% growth
Pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their own stores. Selling that capability gives Parcelbird the growth and leaves the operating risk with grocers

Decisions requested: (1) do not launch in 2027; (2) approve $0.8M/yr for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires, focused on a store-based fast-delivery module; (3) set objective triggers for reopening the question (slide 18).

slides.title: We started from the founders' case for launching and listed five things that would have to be true. The evidence fails four of them and only partly supports the first

claims.claim: Starting hypothesis (the founders' view): “Launch Parcelbird Now: a 15-minute dark-store service in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City, reaching positive contribution per order by month 18.”
1. The market is large, growing and leaves profit for a new entrant — Partly met
evidence: Growing 41%/yr, but Zipcart (−$1.90/order) and QuickBasket (−$3.40/order) both lose money; QuickBasket shut 4 of 11 cities

claims.claim: 2. A Parcelbird order is profitable at performance it can realistically achieve — Not met
evidence: −$6.17 per order at the benchmark median, −$1.76 at the best composite. Positive only if all four plan inputs beat the best site

claims.claim: 3. Customers stay and repay their acquisition cost — Not met
evidence: 22% still ordering at month 3; $38 CAC never repaid at benchmark economics; pop-up demand was promotion-led (12% of AOV)

claims.claim: 4. It can be funded from $12.0M while keeping ≥12 months of runway — Not met
evidence: Floor breached in month 2 (month 11 even if the $9.5M is all-in); cash runs out in month 15; no new round expected

claims.claim: 5. It is the best use of the cash available — Not met
evidence: Software path reaches break-even in about month 26, with runway never below 24 months, and sells into the same q-commerce trend

claims.claim: Revised answer: do not launch in 2027. The hypothesis fails on economics (A) and affordability (B), and a better alternative exists (C).

slides.title: Quick commerce grows about 41% a year, yet its two incumbents lost $406M in 2025. The growth has not created a profit pool

claims.claim: US quick-commerce grocery GMV grows about 41% a year
evidence: Year-on-year growth +44%, +38%, +42%
“Growing over 40% a year” holds: the 2022–25 CAGR is 41.5%, though 2024 grew only 38%

claims.claim: Its two incumbents lost $406M in 2025
evidence: Zipcart (national): Revenue $1,200M, EBITDA −$310M, margin −26%, contribution/order −$1.90
QuickBasket (regional): Revenue $210M, EBITDA −$96M, margin −46%, contribution/order −$3.40
Combined EBITDA −$406M on $1,410M revenue = −29% margin

claims.claim: “Nobody owns the Midwest” is more likely a warning than a gap. The regional player most like Parcelbird closed 36% of its cities in 2025
Market growth does not test the decision. The test is whether one order can make money
Parcelbird's median order-level result (−$2.67) sits between the two incumbents, which supports using the benchmarks

slides.title: At the median performance of Parcelbird's 14 customer sites, each order loses $2.67 before site costs and $6.17 after them

claims.claim: Goods margin on a $34 basket is $9.18. Riders alone cost $7.40 of that, so the basket is too small to carry a 15-minute delivery
evidence: Goods margin 27% × $34 = +$9.18
Delivery fee (net) +$1.99
Promotions 6% × $34 = −$2.04
Picking & packing −$3.10
Payment & packaging −$1.30

claims.claim: Before any store cost, the variable costs already exceed the margin by $2.67
evidence: Order-level contribution −$2.67

claims.claim: Spreading the $1.15M dark-store cost over 900 orders a day adds another $3.50
evidence: Site fixed cost $1.15M ÷ 328.5k = −$3.50
Site-level contribution −$6.17

claims.claim: At this rate one store loses $2.0M a year (−$6.17 × 900 × 365)
Decision metric: site-level contribution, because Parcelbird would own the store costs

slides.title: Only the founders' plan makes money per order, and it needs all four drivers to beat the best site Parcelbird has observed at the same time

claims.claim: Only the founders' plan makes money per order
evidence: Site-level contribution: pop-up −$12.57, benchmark median −$6.17, best observed (composite) −$1.76, founders' plan +$2.02
Order-level (before site cost): pop-up −$6.21, median −$2.67, best +$0.49, plan +$3.77

claims.claim: The plan needs a basket 32% larger than the median, promotions at a third of what every site spends, riders 46% more productive and twice the density, all at once
evidence: AOV: median $34, best $42, pop-up $31, plan $45 (+7% vs best)
Promotions: median 6%, best 6%, pop-up 12%, plan 2% (⅓ of any site)
Orders per rider-hour: median 2.4, best 3.0 (top of range), pop-up 2.1, plan 3.5 (+17% vs best)
Orders per site per day: median 900, best 1,400 (top of range), pop-up 280, plan 1,800 (+29% vs best)
Benchmark ranges: 1.9–3.0 orders per rider-hour; 400–1,400 orders/site/day

claims.claim: Even with every other plan input, standard 6% promotions cut the plan to +$0.22 per order
Best observed is a composite: the best AOV and the best density come from different sites, and no site achieved both.

slides.title: Four optimistic assumptions make up the $8.19 gap between the plan and benchmark reality, and basket size and rider productivity together account for $5.07 of it

claims.claim: Basket size is the largest gap (−$2.75). The pop-up's AOV was $31, so baskets are moving away from $45, not towards it
evidence: Founders' plan +$2.02; AOV $45 → $34: −$2.75

claims.claim: Rider productivity (−$2.32) is the cost line most exposed to the minimum-pay rules under discussion in two of the three cities
evidence: Rider output 3.5 → 2.4/h: −$2.32

claims.claim: Density (−$1.75) depends on demand that the pop-up has not yet shown (280/day, about 410/day at exit)
Promotions 2% → 6% step
evidence: promotions are worth $1.80 at a $45 basket but $1.36 at $34
Benchmark median −$6.17

claims.claim: Closing the gap would need all four to improve together. No site has even combined the best AOV with the best density

slides.title: Even at the best density any site has reached, no combination of observed basket size and rider productivity breaks even with standard promotions

claims.claim: Every cell is negative at 1,400 orders/day and 6% promotions
evidence: At 1,800/day (above any site) only the plan's own AOV and rider productivity turn positive: +$0.22.

claims.claim: Break-even needs a basket well above anything seen, or density and productivity above the top of the benchmark range
evidence: Break-even AOV at median density & riders: $63 (observed max $42)
AOV at best density & riders: $50 (max $42)
AOV at plan density & riders, 6% promos: $44 (max $42)
Orders per rider-hour at median AOV & density: 14.4 (max 3.0)
Break-even AOV solves AOV × (27% − 6%) = $2.41 + rider cost + site fixed cost per order

claims.claim: The economics depend on the format itself (small basket, paid rider, dedicated store). Better execution alone will not fix them

slides.title: Parcelbird's own pop-up trailed its customers' median on all four drivers, so the evidence does not yet support “we run them better than anyone”

claims.claim: Pop-up trailed the median on all four drivers
evidence: AOV: pop-up $31, median $34, plan $45
Promotions: pop-up 12%, median 6%, plan 2%
Orders per rider-hour: pop-up 2.1, median 2.4, plan 3.5
Orders per site per day: pop-up 280, median 900, plan 1,800

claims.claim: Order-level loss of $6.21 and site-level loss of $12.57 per order; about $0.15M lost over six weeks
evidence: Pop-up: six weeks, one temporary site, autumn 2026, 11,800 orders

claims.claim: The 12% promotions and first-order credits bought much of the 18%/week order growth
Fair caveats: Six weeks at a temporary site is an early read, and volume was still rising (about 410/day at exit). Still, exit volume was below the 900/day median, and the plan assumes 1,800/day
evidence: week 1 ≈ 1,250 orders, week 6 ≈ 2,860 orders (≈ 410/day)

slides.title: Zipcart's one profitable city shows what break-even costs: a $3.99 fee and almost no promotions, which cost 14% of volume. The same moves would still leave Parcelbird at −$1.05

claims.claim: Zipcart's densest city, Q4 2025, reached break-even by charging more and losing customers
evidence: Contribution per order after changes +$0.40
New service fee on every order +$3.99
Promotions cut to 1% of order value
Order volume afterwards −14%
Implied contribution without the new fee (if fully retained) ≈ −$3.59
Zipcart national contribution per order −$1.90

claims.claim: The founders read this as “it can be done”. The shareholder letter says it was done by charging customers more and losing customers, and only in Zipcart's densest city. Nationally it still loses $1.90 per order.
Even if Parcelbird copies Zipcart's moves, its stores stay loss-making. Order-level contribution would turn positive (+$3.02), but the dark-store fixed cost would not be covered.
evidence: Benchmark median −$6.17; +$3.99 service fee; promotions 6% → 1% +$1.70; volume −14% (fixed cost/order) −$0.57; with Zipcart's levers −$1.05
$1.15M site cost over 774 orders/day ($4.07/order)

slides.title: Pop-up demand was largely bought: 22% of customers still ordered at month 3, and the $38 acquisition cost is never repaid at benchmark economics

claims.claim: Stated intent exceeds revealed behaviour; demand was promotion-led
evidence: 44% of surveyed 25–39-year-olds said they would use it at least weekly (stated intent)
22% of pop-up customers still ordering in month 3 (revealed behaviour)
$38 customer acquisition cost (paid social and first-order credits)
12% of AOV spent on promotions in the pop-up, twice the benchmark

claims.claim: The $38 acquisition cost is never repaid at benchmark economics
evidence: Benchmark median: −$2.67 order-level, −$1.82 monthly per acquired customer, payback Never
Best observed: +$0.49, +$0.34, ≈ 113 months
Founders' plan: +$3.77, +$2.57, ≈ 15 months
Monthly per acquired customer = 22% × 3.1 orders × order-level contribution. At site level the plan's payback stretches to about 28 months.

claims.claim: Acquisition spend needed to fill nine stores
evidence: Benchmark 900/day $13.5M; best observed 1,400/day $21.1M; founders' plan 1,800/day $27.1M; total plan budget $9.5M
At plan density each store needs about 79,000 acquired customers (≈ $3.0M of CAC). The $9.5M plan covers capex, marketing and losses together.

slides.title: The $9.5M plan breaks the 12-month runway floor within its first year under either reading of the budget. If it adds to today's burn, cash runs out in month 15

claims.claim: Both launch readings breach the 12-month runway floor; software path never does
evidence: Scale software: floor never breached (min 24 mo.), cash at month 18 $6.0M
Launch, $9.5M on top: floor breached month 2, cash at month 18 −$2.3M (out in month 15)
Launch, $9.5M all-in: floor breached month 11, cash at month 18 $2.5M
Runway chart (months): launch on top 30 → 12.09 (m1) → 11.24 (m2) → 0 at m15; all-in 21.74 (m1) → 11.74 (m11) → 4.74 (m18); software min 23.86 (m8), capped at 36

claims.claim: The pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes the software burn. We assume it does not (base case) and test the generous reading too
Without the launch, the software business already uses about $6.6M of cash before break-even
The plan is costed on the founders' inputs; at benchmark inputs the loss is larger

slides.title: At benchmark economics the nine stores would need about $37M in their first full year. Even a one-store pilot keeps runway below the floor for over a year

claims.claim: Cash needed vs. available
evidence: Cash in the bank $12.0M
Founders' plan (to month 18) $9.5M: capex $5.4M, marketing & losses $4.1M
Benchmark economics (first full year) $37.1M: operating loss $18.2M, CAC $13.5M, capex $5.4M
Operating loss = −$6.17 × 900 orders × 365 days × 9 stores. CAC = $1.50M per store × 9.

claims.claim: Smaller operator bets break the floor or teach nothing new
evidence: One permanent dark store, 12 months: ≈ $3.8M; below 12 mo. from month 5 to 18 (low 6.3); Little new: 14 customer sites and the pop-up already show the economics
Second pop-up: ≈ $0.15M per 6 weeks; within floor; Repeats a test already run, still at a loss

claims.claim: Other risks that make it worse
evidence: Rider minimum-pay rules (two of three cities): each +$1/hour costs $0.42 per order at 2.4 orders/hour, about $1.2M a year across nine stores
No new funding round is expected for a delivery operator, so any shortfall has to come out of the software business
Operating would compete with grocers who are customers or prospects, which puts the $96k-a-year contracts at risk

slides.title: The software business already has a funded path to growth: its pipeline is worth 1.4× the ARR that 60% growth needs in 2027, and the proposed hires pay back with about 11 contracts

claims.claim: Pipeline is worth 1.4× the ARR that 60% growth needs in 2027
evidence: Total pipeline (37 grocers) $3.55M; late-stage pipeline (9) $0.86M; new ARR for 60% growth in 2027 $2.46M; new ARR for 45% growth $1.84M
60% growth needs about 26 new contracts in 2027. The 9 late-stage deals cover a third of that, so 17 must come from the 28 earlier-stage grocers or new leads.

claims.claim: Hires pay back with about 11 contracts
evidence: Hire payback = $0.8M ÷ ($96k × 81% gross margin) = 10.3 contracts per year. Assumes no churn and no expansion revenue.

claims.claim: Software vs Parcelbird Now economics
evidence: Gross margin: 81% vs 27% on goods; order loses money
Unit of growth: $96k contract, ≈ $78k gross profit/yr vs order at −$6.17
Capital per unit: hiring; no capex vs $0.6M capex + $1.5M CAC per store
Who bears operating risk: the grocer vs Parcelbird

claims.claim: Captures q-commerce growth without the operator's losses
evidence: Several pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their existing stores. A store-based module fits Parcelbird's picking and rider-dispatch software
Store-based delivery uses stores the grocer already pays for, avoiding the $3.50/order dark-store cost (not quantified in the pack)
Parcelbird keeps learning from more sites without putting its own capital at risk

slides.title: Scaling software reaches cash break-even in about month 26 and stays above the runway floor at 45% growth. Only a fall to about 30% would need cost action

claims.claim: Scaling software reaches cash break-even in about month 26 and stays above the runway floor at 45% growth
evidence: 60% growth (base): break-even month 26, lowest cash $5.4M, floor held
45% growth: month 32, $3.6M, held
60%, opex +10%/yr: month 32, $3.1M, held
30% growth (stress): month 46, runs out, breached m23
Cash chart ($M): 60% path from 12 to low ≈5.39 at month 25, 10.90 at month 42; 45% path low ≈3.58 at month 31; 30% path falls to 0.035 at month 42

claims.claim: At 30% growth, runway falls below 12 months around month 23 and cash runs out near month 46
The board can see this early: if ARR growth runs below about 45% by mid-2027, cut opex to hold the floor
Even in the stress case Parcelbird keeps 23 months to act, compared with 2 months in the launch case
evidence: Implied opex = $4.1M × 81% + $4.8M burn = $8.1M/yr, held flat in real terms, plus $0.8M hires

slides.title: Of the four options, only scaling software with a store-based delivery module meets both board constraints and still captures quick-commerce growth

claims.claim: A. Launch as planned (9 dark stores, 3 cities): Reject
evidence: Path to profit: No: −$6.17/order at median; +$2.02 only on plan inputs
Runway: No: breached in month 2 (month 11 if all-in)
Exposure: Direct, but at a loss on every order
Downside: Company-ending: cash out in month 15
Reversibility: Low: leases, capex, brand

claims.claim: B. Single-store pilot (Columbus, 12 months): Reject
evidence: No: about −$3.8M; no path to profit at one store
No: below floor from month 5 to 18
Exposure: Small
Uses about a third of cash for little new learning
Reversibility: Medium

claims.claim: C. Scale software + store-based delivery module: Recommend
evidence: Yes: break-even in about month 26 (base)
Yes: min 24 months (base), 20 at 45% growth
Indirect: grocers' fast-delivery demand
Slower growth; cut opex if growth is under 45%
High: can still operate later

claims.claim: D. Status quo (no hires, no launch): Fallback
evidence: Likely, but slower if the pipeline is not converted
Runway: Yes
Limited to current customers
Pipeline left to competitors
Reversibility: High

claims.claim: A hybrid (license software and run stores) is covered by A/B, because the store losses are the same.

slides.title: The recommendation rests on a few explicit assumptions. The one that matters most is software growth holding above about 45%

claims.claim: Key assumptions tested; answer changes only if Parcelbird beat the best site on all four drivers at once
evidence: Benchmark sites represent what Parcelbird Now would achieve: 14 customer sites + pop-up; pop-up was worse
Density: No: break-even fails even at 1,400/day
AOV: No: break-even AOV is $44–$63 with 6% promotions
Rider labor rules: Reinforces it: −$0.42/order per +$1/hour
$9.5M excludes software burn: No: floor breached in month 11 even if all-in
Software ARR grows 60%: No, but at 30% cost action is needed by about month 20
Store-based module demand: No: upside only, not needed for break-even
Founder motivation and focus: Not modelled; execution risk to software plan

slides.title: We ask the board to make three decisions in January and to set measurable triggers for reopening the operator question

claims.claim: 1. Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. No dark-store leases, capex or launch marketing, and no further pop-ups.
2. Fund software scaling: $0.8M a year. 2 engineers and 2 sales hires; target ≥11 new contracts per year to pay back the hires.
3. Build a store-based fast-delivery module with 2–3 design-partner grocers from the late-stage pipeline; price as an add-on to the $96k contract.
Reopen the operator question only if all of these hold
evidence: A real site is positive at site level for 2 straight quarters, with promotions ≥ 5% and no extra fee: ≥ $0 / order; today best composite −$1.76
Software business is self-funding: burn ≤ 0 for a quarter; today burn $0.4M / month
Cash after a launch still gives ≥ 12 months of runway: fully funded plan; today not met
Rider pay rules in the target cities are known: rules final; today under consideration

claims.claim: On the base case the software business reaches break-even in early 2029. Parcelbird could then revisit operating from a position of strength, with benchmark data from many more customer sites.

slides.title: Appendix 1. Unit economics calculations for all four scenarios

claims.claim: Unit economics for pop-up / benchmark median / best observed / founders' plan
evidence: Delivery fee: +$1.99 all
Picking & packing: −$3.10 all
Payment & packaging: −$1.30 all
Order-level contribution: −$6.21 / −$2.67 / +$0.49 / +$3.77

Site-level contribution: −$12.57 / −$6.17 / −$1.76 / +$2.02

slides.title: Appendix 2. Cash and runway model: method and assumptions

claims.claim: Method
evidence: Monthly model from January 2027, starting at the $12.0M stated in the pack
Software ARR compounds monthly; revenue = ARR ÷ 12; gross margin 81%
Implied opex: $4.1M × 81% = $3.32M gross profit + $4.8M annual burn = $8.12M/yr, held flat in real terms (stress case: +10%/yr)
Hires add $0.8M/yr (option C). Status quo (D) has no hires and assumes slower pipeline conversion
Runway = cash ÷ that month's net burn. The board rule is ≥12 months at all times
Launch (base reading): $9.5M spread evenly over 18 months on top of software burn, no hires
Launch (all-in reading): $9.5M covers all company spending for 18 months
Pilot: one store, $0.6M capex in month 1, $1.15M fixed, 600 orders/day average at −$2.67, $1.5M CAC over 12 months

claims.claim: Outputs
evidence: Months to break-even, 60% / 45% / 30% growth: 26 / 32 / 46
Lowest cash, 60% / 45% growth: $5.4M / $3.6M
Lowest runway, 60% / 45% growth: 24 / 20 months
Launch on top: floor breach / cash-out: Month 2 / month 15
Launch all-in: floor breach / cash at m18: Month 11 / $2.5M
Pilot: months below floor: 5 to 18 (low 6.3 months)
CAC to fill 9 stores at 900 / 1,400 / 1,800 per day: $13.5M / $21.1M / $27.1M
Benchmark nine-store annual operating loss: $18.2M

slides.title: Appendix 3. Where the briefing pack was ambiguous, we chose the reading that is most favourable to launching or most standard, and tested the alternative

claims.claim: Ambiguity choices do not change the answer
evidence: Contribution per order incl. fixed costs? Show both levels; decide on site level. None: the median is negative at both levels (−$2.67 / −$6.17)
Does the $9.5M include software burn? Base: no; also tested all-in. None: floor breached in month 2 or month 11
Best observed site as composite (generous to launch). None: still −$1.76 per order
44% survey: stated intent from 25–39s only; use pop-up retention (22%). Weakens the demand case
Software 60% growth: assume $0.8M hires sustain 60%; stress at 45% and 30%. Recommendation holds; cost action needed only near 30%
Cash at January 2027: $12.0M as stated (Nov–Dec 2026 burn ignored). All paths about $0.8M lower; ranking unchanged

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 (no dark-store leases, capex or launch marketing, and no further pop-ups). Put the money into the software business: fund software scaling at $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires (target ≥11 new contracts per year), and build a store-based fast-delivery module with 2–3 design-partner grocers from the late-stage pipeline, priced as an add-on to the $96k contract. Set measurable triggers for reopening the operator question.

Reject: about −$3.8M; no path to profit at one store; below floor from month 5 to 18; uses about a third of cash for little new learning.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Scale software + store-based delivery module

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Benchmark sites represent what Parcelbird Now would achieve (14 customer sites + pop-up; pop-up was worse); answer changes only if Parcelbird beat the best site on all four drivers at once
Density in mid-size Midwest cities: median 900/day; pop-up 280 (≈410 at exit); break-even fails even at 1,400/day
AOV can rise without losing the convenience use case: range $31–$45 tested; break-even AOV is $44–$63 with 6% promotions
Rider labor rules (2 of 3 cities) not in base case; reinforces answer: −$0.42/order per +$1/hour
$9.5M excludes software burn (base case); all-in reading also tested; ask founders to confirm budget scope
Software ARR grows 60% with $0.8M hires; tested at 45% and 30% and opex +10%/yr; at 30% cost action needed by about month 20. The one that matters most is software growth holding above about 45%
Store-based module demand is qualitative ("several grocers"); upside only, not needed for break-even; avoided dark-store cost not quantified in the pack
Founder motivation and focus not modelled; execution risk to software plan
Best observed is a composite of different sites (generous to launch)
44% survey is stated intent from 25–39s only; pop-up retention (22%) used as revealed behaviour
Cash at January 2027 taken as $12.0M (Nov–Dec 2026 burn ignored); all paths about $0.8M lower
CAC calculation assumes survivors stay and no organic acquisition (both generous); payback ignores orders in months 1–2
Hire payback assumes no churn and no expansion revenue
Pop-up was six weeks at a temporary site, an early read, with volume still rising
All figures are synthetic benchmark data from the briefing pack
next_steps: Weeks 1–4: hire plan approved; first design-partner grocer signed for the module
Weeks 4–8: close as many of the 9 late-stage deals as possible (≈ $0.86M ARR)
Week 12: board review of ARR growth, burn and runway against the base case
Validate store-based module demand with 9 late-stage grocers in Q1
Quarterly ARR review; pre-agreed opex cuts if ARR growth runs below about 45% by mid-2027
Ask founders to confirm budget scope of the $9.5M

Reopen operator question only if all triggers hold: a real site positive at site level for 2 straight quarters (promotions ≥5%, no extra fee); software self-funding (burn ≤0 for a quarter); ≥12 months runway after a launch; rider pay rules final in target cities
